description: We are FireFlyers, a team from Brazil that turns big challenges into simple, useful ideas. Like fireflies, we believe small lights shine brighter together. We value creativity, practical problem-solving and quick adaptation when plans change. We mix science, design and technology to build clear, accessible tools.
summary:
Far from Earth, astronauts have to take care of their own health. In orbit they lose about 1% of bone density per month, in deep space they receive up to 1.8 mSv of radiation per day, and from Mars a reply from Earth can take 22 minutes. Core Leonis is a web app that helps crews monitor their health every day and act correctly in an emergency.

How it answers the challenge:
- Astronauts enter their own data (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood and dosimeter readings) and see each value as normal, watch or alert, with trend charts.
- A clickable human figure shows which body areas need care.
- Orbit, Moon, Mars and Deep Space each have their own gravity, radiation, communication delay, missions and emergency advice.
- Daily missions based on NASA countermeasures, with steps, timers and equipment guides, plus streaks and milestones to keep the routine going.
- 23 emergency decision trees give clear instructions for non-experts in a few yes/no answers.

The same routine also works on Earth, against inactivity and sun damage: 31% of adults worldwide (40.9% in Brazil, where our team lives) are not active enough, and UV causes 83% of melanoma cases.

All figures come from NASA, CSA and WHO sources listed in the app. It runs in any browser, with no install or account.
details:
Overview

Core Leonis is a health-monitoring app built for astronauts: crews in Low Earth Orbit, on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It helps them follow their daily countermeasures, monitor their own health and act correctly in an emergency, especially when Earth is too far away to help in real time. The same science also works at home, so Core Leonis includes an Earth mode that helps anyone fight inactivity and sun damage. Its name comes from Cor Leonis, “the heart of the lion”, the old name of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo, because the app protects the heart of every crew: its body, its mind and its ability to act under pressure. It runs in any browser, needs no install or account, and works on a phone or tablet.

The problem astronauts face

Spaceflight is hard on the human body, and it gets harder the farther crews travel:

  • Bones and muscles: even with about two hours of exercise a day, astronauts lose around 1% of their bone density per month, roughly what an older adult loses in a year.
  • Eyes and circulation: about 70% of astronauts on 6–12-month ISS missions show eye changes caused by fluid shifting toward the head (SANS).
  • Radiation: doses reach 0.2–0.5 mSv per day on the ISS, about 1.37 on the Moon’s surface and about 1.8 in deep space, against a NASA career limit of 600 mSv.
  • Distance: from Mars, a message takes up to 22 minutes each way, so a reply can take 44 minutes. Bringing a patient home takes hours from the ISS, about 3 days from the Moon and months from Mars.
  • Isolation, confinement and disrupted sleep: the ISS sees 16 sunrises a day, and a Mars day lasts about 24 h 39 min.

NASA groups these into five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile, closed environments. On future missions, crews will have to monitor themselves and solve medical problems on their own. Core Leonis is designed for exactly that.

What it does for crews

The astronaut chooses where the mission is and works through six connected parts:

  • Environments: Low Earth Orbit, Moon, Mars and Deep Space each have their own gravity, radiation per day, message delay and time to medical help. The missions, radiation thresholds and emergency advice all change to match. A Compare view shows all environments side by side, and Earth is included as a reference.
  • Today, the daily countermeasures: missions based on NASA research, including resistive and aerobic training, a fluid-shift and vision check with thigh cuffs, nutrition and hydration, a sleep routine with wrist actigraphy, crew connection, morning vitals and a dosimeter check. Each mission has checkable steps, built-in timers and how-to guides for the hardware: the resistive exercise device, the treadmill with bungee harness, the cycle ergometer, compact flywheel devices, thigh cuffs, pulse oximeter, blood-pressure cuff, telemedicine monitor and dosimeter. Notes explain what changes in each place: on the Moon, walking in 1/6 g is not enough to load your bones; in a small deep-space capsule, a compact flywheel replaces large machines. Each environment also has its own missions: a pre-spacewalk health check, a balance and gaze drill for gravity transitions, and dust control after spacewalks on the Moon and Mars; autonomy planning and a medical-kit review for Mars; a radiation-shelter drill for deep space.
  • Body: an interactive body map with five regions (mind and sleep, heart and circulation, nutrition, muscles and bones, radiation shield). Each region changes color with the care it receives and fades without it, faster in microgravity, making deconditioning visible. The map suggests a focus mission for the weakest region.
  • Health, self-monitoring: the astronaut logs heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood, following the idea of NASA’s Standard Measures (a consistent set of data from every crew member). Each value gets a typical, watch or alert status and a trend chart, with a step-by-step guide for the measuring device. An alert offers the matching emergency tree right away.
  • SOS, emergency guidance without waiting for Earth: 23 decision trees grouped as life-threatening, urgent and care. In space they cover:
    ◦ an unresponsive crewmate (including CPR in microgravity);
    ◦ chest pain and low oxygen;
    ◦ fire, smoke and toxic leaks;
    ◦ radiation alarms and solar particle events, including recalling crew from a spacewalk;
    ◦ decompression sickness after a spacewalk;
    ◦ lunar and Martian dust exposure;
    ◦ bleeding, burns and eye injuries from floating particles;
    ◦ space motion sickness, dizziness after gravity changes, and crew behavioral health. Questions use objective criteria (“SpO₂ below 90%?”, “Look at the chest for 10 seconds: breathing normally?”). Results start with the action, show how fast to act (“Start within 1 minute”) and adapt to where the crew is. Near Earth, the result says “flight surgeons answer almost in real time”; on the Moon, “stabilise on site, home is 3 days away”; on Mars, “act first and report after, Earth cannot guide you live”.
  • Radiation, the crew’s own dose log: the astronaut enters the value shown on their dosimeter and gets a status gauge, recommended actions, a dose history and an estimated mission dose. What counts as “nominal” depends on the environment, and an alert level sends the crew to the radiation-shelter procedure. A Help page explains the measuring devices: personal dosimeters, CSA’s bubble detectors used on the ISS, and the CANS neutron spectrometer now in development, which will measure neutrons continuously (about 30% of the ISS dose).

The pages work together: an alert in Health opens the right SOS tree, logging the dosimeter completes the radiation mission, and every mission strengthens a body region.

A day on a mission with Core Leonis

On Mars, an astronaut opens the app in the morning and sees today’s conditions: 0.38 g, about 0.7 mSv per day, a 3–22-minute delay and months to medical help. They log heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen, which completes the morning-vitals mission. They read their dosimeter, enter the value and confirm it is nominal. During training, the timer guides the intervals and the equipment guide reminds them how to anchor the device. After a spacewalk, the dust-control mission walks them through cleaning the suit in the airlock. If a crewmate suddenly reports joint pain and numbness, the SOS tree identifies possible decompression sickness in two questions and lists what to do now, starting with 100% oxygen, without waiting 44 minutes for an answer from Earth. At night, completed missions light up as stars, and the streak keeps the routine going for the months ahead.

How it addresses the challenge

The challenge asked for software that helps astronauts monitor their health from data they enter, works in different space environments and can be used by non-experts. Core Leonis covers each part:

  • Self-entered health indicators with clear status and trends.
  • A clickable human figure.
  • Gamification that supports consistency.
  • Distinct space environments.
  • Simple, step-by-step instructions for daily care and emergencies.

Impact in space and on Earth

In space, Core Leonis gives crews a single place for countermeasures, consistent self-measurement and emergency guidance. Missions to the Moon and Mars will need exactly this kind of autonomy. Consistent logs also give flight surgeons better data when contact is possible.

On Earth, the same science helps everyone. Weightlessness mimics a sedentary life, and 31% of adults worldwide (1.8 billion people) don’t get enough physical activity, rising to 40.9% in Brazil, where our team lives. UV causes 83% of melanoma cases, and skin cancer is the most common cancer in Brazil. Earth mode turns astronaut routines into brisk walks, strength circuits, breaks from sitting and a sunscreen streak with reapply reminders. WHO estimates that 4–5 million deaths a year could be averted with more activity, and in a randomized trial daily sunscreen use halved melanomas. Because the app runs in any phone browser with no account, it can reach people regardless of their device or budget.

Scientific foundation

Every mission, threshold and figure is linked to a source on the in-app Science & sources page:

  • NASA Human Research Program: the five hazards and studies such as Zero T2, Thigh Cuff, B-Complex, ARCHeR, Standard Measures, Tempus Pro, Food Acceptability, Space Gardening and manual piloting for Moon landings.
  • NASA technical reports and Curiosity RAD measurements (ISS, transit, Mars).
  • Chang’e 4 measurements (Moon).
  • Canadian Space Agency data on exercise and radiation monitoring (bubble detectors and CANS).
  • WHO, IARC, the Nambour sunscreen trial and Brazilian national data for Earth mode.

Creativity and design

We treated health monitoring as a daily routine, not a game. There are no points, levels or quizzes: only streaks, milestones and a constellation that lights up as missions are completed, echoing the star behind the name. The logo is a heart-shaped constellation with Regulus at its tip. Smooth animations, sounds synthesized in the browser and haptics on mobile make logging data feel rewarding, which matters on long missions where motivation is a real challenge. Explanations sit behind small info buttons and sources on their own page, so screens stay clean and fast to read.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks, build step or server. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages. Sound effects use the Web Audio API, and data stays only on the device (localStorage). All content (environments, missions, equipment guides, vital signs, SOS trees, radiation thresholds and sources) lives in a single file, so flight surgeons or scientists can add or adjust protocols without programming. We checked every decision tree automatically to make sure no answer leads to a dead end, and tested the app on phone-sized screens.

Factors we considered

  • Use under stress: short yes/no questions, the action first, and time to act on every result.
  • Autonomy: advice adapts to communication delay and evacuation time in each environment.
  • Scientific honesty: cited sources, and clear labels where values are simplified for demonstration (reference ranges, radiation thresholds and the body-decay model).
  • Privacy: no account, and no data leaves the device.
  • Accessibility: runs on simple devices, respects reduced-motion settings and keeps contrast high.
  • Safety: Core Leonis is an educational prototype, not a medical device. Real crews follow flight-surgeon procedures, and on Earth the first step in an emergency is always calling the local emergency number.

What’s next

  • Read data directly from crew wearables and dosimeters instead of typing it in.
  • Export health records for the flight surgeon.
  • A fully offline mode for missions with limited contact.
  • Validating the decision trees with space-medicine and healthcare professionals.
  • Portuguese and Spanish versions for Earth users.
